newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean firms issue bonds to fend off raiders.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean firms issue bonds to fend off raiders.

text.p: South Korean companies are hastily throwing up defences against potential hostile takeovers ahead of legal changes next month that will make it more difficult to fend off predators.
Dozens of companies have issued equity-linked bonds to management or friendly outsiders, and many more are planning to do so by April 1, stock exchange officials said on Friday.
Bonds convertible into common stock, or bonds with stock warrants attached, in the hands of management would act as a powerful deterrent to corporate predators.
"Companies have recently started issuing bonds to defend against any possible takeovers," said Lim Choon-soo, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets Ltd.
But regulations due to take effect on April 1 will bar companies from privately placing such bonds "in the course of management disputes" -- a clear reference to hostile takeover attempts.
A Korea Stock Exchange official said 33 companies privately placed 645.5 billion won ($722.9 million) worth of such paper as of Thursday. No similar issues were reported to the exchange last year.
Some companies were jolted into action by South Korea's first big hostile takeover bid this month when edible oil maker Shindongbang Corp made a grab for fashionable retailer Midopa Department Store.
To ward off the unwelcome attention, Midopa issued bonds with warrants.
The raid on Midopa fizzled, but authorities subsequently announced the curbs on equity-linked bond issues.
Many companies have been gripped by takeover fears since the government in January lifted a 10 percent ceiling on individual stock holdings.
The aim was to encourage mergers and acquisitions, until now virtually unheard of.
Equity-linked bonds give holders the option to purchase a specified number of shares at a set price and within a certain period.
"The number of privately placed bond issues will increase this month as more companies try to protect managerial rights," said one stock exchange official.

The new regulations also specify that the conversion price for equity-linked bonds should not be below the market price at the time of issue. And holders will not be able to exercise conversion rights for one year.
Currently, there are no specific regulations governing pricing and the conversion period.
Analysts said mergers and acquisitions would hone the competitiveness of South Korean companies, typically owned and managed by families.

Samchully Corp, a city gas supplier, privately placed 30 billion won of convertible bonds on Wednesday to two local insurance companies. If fully converted, the issue would boost the company's share capital by 15.6 percent.
"Company owners, especially of smaller companies, don't feel comfortable with their existing stake," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
"They are trying to make their management rock solid."
He said management ownership of listed companies averaged 23 to 25 percent.
